subject: religious-studies
title: The Ontological Tower
welcome_lead: Climb the spiral tower of pure thought where Anselm, Descartes, and Plantinga argue from concept to existence.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on ontological arguments.
final_note: From the idea of God alone, can we leap to His being? The tower keeps the question alive.

concepts.def: An a priori argument that moves from the concept of God to His necessary existence.
From Proslogion 2: God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived must exist in reality, not merely in the understanding.
From Proslogion 3: God cannot be conceived not to exist; necessary existence is a perfection.
In Meditation V (1641), God's existence follows from His essence as a supremely perfect being, just as triangles necessarily have three angles.
In the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), Kant argued that 'existence is not a predicate'.
If it is possible that a maximally great being exists, then such a being exists in every possible world, including the actual one.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Anselm (1033-1109) addresses the fool of Psalm 14 who says 'there is no God'. Even the fool understands the concept 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived', so it exists in his understanding.

But a being existing in reality is greater than one existing only in the understanding. Therefore, the greatest conceivable being must exist in reality, lest a contradiction follow.

The monk Gaunilo responded 'On Behalf of the Fool' with a parody: by the same logic, the greatest conceivable island must exist, since otherwise a greater could be conceived.

Anselm replied that the argument applies only to a being whose essence includes necessary existence; the parody fails because islands are essentially contingent.

In the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), Kant argued that 'being' is not a real predicate that adds anything to the concept of a thing.

'A hundred real thalers do not contain the least coin more than a hundred possible thalers.' Existence cannot be derived from a concept alone, so ontological arguments fail.
